analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires prevailing wages on federally funded construction.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 79 House members, died in committee without ever getting a vote, leaving federal construction wage rules in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act, passed in 1931, requires contractors on federally financed construction to pay workers the locally prevailing wage. This bill would repeal that law outright, effective 30 days after enactment, so contractors on federal projects could pay whatever wage the market allowed. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Contractors and subcontractors on federally funded construction would gain, because they could bid lower labor costs and keep the difference. Taxpayers might see slightly lower federal construction bids, though research on prevailing-wage rules is contested.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, ending the requirement that laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction be paid the locally prevailing wage [S2][S3].
The repeal would take effect 30 days after enactment and would not disturb existing contracts or bids already outstanding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects, who could see their pay drop toward market lows in areas where prevailing wages had been lifted by union-scale standards.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the prevailing-wage floor would remove the wage protection that keeps contractors from undercutting local standards with low-paid crews on federal jobs [S2].
The repeal takes effect quickly — 30 days after enactment — giving workers on upcoming federal projects no transition period, though contracts already in place would be honored [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Contractors would clearly gain from lower labor costs on federal work. Workers on those projects would likely lose pay, and communities built around prevailing-wage standards could see wages drift down. The bill offered no offsetting protection for workers, making the trade simple: savings for government buyers and contractors, lower wages for the crews doing the work.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor Standards Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Stenholm and 45 original cosponsors introduced the bill on April 11, 1991; it would repeal the 1931 Davis-Bacon Act outright [S3].
A total of 79 members cosponsored it — 71 Republicans and 8 Democrats [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced [S5][S1].
On May 10, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where it remained; no further action appears in the record before the 102nd Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers and their unions, since the federal prevailing-wage floor stayed intact when the bill died in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers, whose federal wage floor survived

for.name: Rep. Charles W. Stenholm
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act on April 11, 1991 [S1][S3].

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it was referred to a subcommittee on May 10, 1991 and never advanced to the full committee or the floor [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was heavily Republican — 71 of 79 cosponsors — with a handful of conservative and moderate Democrats including the sponsor joining.

industries.note: Without the prevailing-wage requirement, contractors could pay lower wages on federally funded projects and bid more aggressively. Their gain would come directly out of construction workers' pay.
The bill would have removed the wage floor protecting laborers and mechanics on federal construction, exposing them to market-low pay. Its defeat preserved that protection.
